$comment: The no-handle answer table, shared by all three test targets.
Every row is a question asked of a file sink that has NO live handle, which
is the whole of FileSinkLifecycle's no-handle contract. The two modes differ
on exactly one bit -- whether files may exist -- and every answer below is
derived from it. Four of these rows once disagreed across the three
implementations, and none of the disagreements was reachable through
FileDestination, which short-circuits first. That is why they survived, and
why the answers now live in one file instead of three suites.
Loaded by:
__tests__/fileSinkLifecycleRows.test.ts        (require)
swift-tests/.../FileSinkLifecycleRowsTests.swift  (#filePath walk-up)
android/src/test/.../FileSinkLifecycleRowsTest.kt (repoRoot system property)
Values are strings on purpose. Three languages have three opinions about
how a number, a boolean and an absent field compare; a string does not.
Each loader renders the real answer's fields to strings and compares those,
so a row reads the same in all three and a failure prints the same in all
three.
## Adding a row or a field
Adding either makes all three suites RED until each implements it. That is
the point of the file: an unmatched op is a failure and never a skip, and a
field a dispatcher produces but the table does not name is also a failure,
so the table cannot silently under-assert. See each loader's guard block.
## What this does NOT prove
That the shipped adapters answer this way. Until the FileSinkAnswers
extraction lands, the native dispatchers derive their answers from
FileSinkLifecycle the way HybridFileSink/HybridFileSink.kt do, rather than
executing those files -- which no unit test on either platform can reach.
The table pins the contract; it does not yet pin the adapter.

modeMeaning.neverOpened: no handle, and nothing can exist yet: vacuous success is honest
modeMeaning.openedThenClosed: no handle, and files may exist: vacuous success is a lie

rows.why: Refused as closed either way. The status fields are zeroed rather than the last ones the handle reported -- there is no handle to ask, and a stale queuedBytes reads as backlog that no flush can ever drain.
Zeroed, both modes. Loss counters belong to a handle; reporting the closed handle's would charge this sink for entries it no longer owns, and reporting them repeatedly would charge it twice.
Same zeroed status, and the sweep must not run. Maintenance belongs to whoever holds the writer now; a closed sink that still prunes deletes another handle's archives.
complete=true is the row that matters, and it is true in both modes. A support flow that read a no-handle collect as a failure would show an error to a user whose app simply has no logs yet.

The first row that splits on the bit. Nothing was ever accepted by a sink that never opened, so there is nothing to vouch for and durable is honest. A closed sink cannot vouch for bytes it handed to a writer it no longer holds.
Idempotent, and a repeat close answers what the first one did. A second close that reported durable=true over the first one's false would let a caller retry its way to a success that never happened.

Nothing was attempted, so nothing failed: a failedPath here reports a deletion failure for a file no one tried to delete. durable splits on the bit -- this is the compliance answer, and claiming it over surviving files is the whole reason the bit exists.

Reads the same bit as clearLogs, and deliberately not artifactSource(): a sink that opened and closed knows where its bundle would be but cannot confirm it is gone, and true there deletes the caller's obligation to retry.

Closing releases a handle; it does not delete files, and the paths have to keep coming back. An empty list from a closed sink tells a support-upload flow there is nothing to collect over logs still sitting on the device.
